deep.reconstruction:
Context: notes from 1953 on Hilbert-space tensor algebra, part of the functional-analysis material around Grothendieck's thesis (tensor products and nuclear spaces). The previous page builds the Hilbert tensor power $\hat\otimes^n E$ and the antisymmetrization projector $a_n$, shown to be an orthogonal (hermitian) projector. It defines the 'puissance extérieure hilbertienne' $\hat\Lambda^{(n)}E$ as the range of $a_n$, with the inner product rescaled by $n!$. With this normalization one gets, on decomposable multivectors, formula (4): $(a_1\wedge\dots\wedge a_n,\, b_1\wedge\dots\wedge b_n)=\det((a_i,b_j))$.

This page states a theorem.
- The algebraic exterior power $\Lambda^n E$ carries a unique positive definite hermitian form satisfying (4).
- Its completion is the Hilbert exterior power.
- If $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ is an orthonormal basis of $E$, the $e_J=e_{i_1}\wedge\dots\wedge e_{i_n}$ ($i_1<\dots<i_n$) form a Hilbert (orthonormal) basis of $\hat\Lambda^n E$.

As a consequence, (5): $\|a_1\wedge\dots\wedge a_n\|=\det((a_i,a_j))^{1/2}\le\|a_1\|\cdots\|a_n\|$, i.e. the norm is the square root of the Gram determinant.

Proof of the inequality:
- Expand $a_i=\sum_j a_{ij}e_j$ and let $A=(a_{ij})$.
- The Gram matrix is $AA^*$, so $\det\mathrm{Gram}=|\det A|^2$.
- The inequality is therefore Hadamard's inequality (6), $|\det A|\le\prod\|a_i\|$: the volume of the parallelotope is at most the product of the edge lengths.
- To prove it, choose the basis (Gram–Schmidt) so that $A$ is triangular. Then $\det A=\prod a_{ii}$ and $|a_{ii}|\le\|a_i\|$.

Corollary: $|\det((a_i,b_j))|\le\prod_i\|a_i\|\,\|b_i\|$. This follows from Cauchy–Schwarz in $\hat\Lambda^n E$ combined with (5).

Purpose: these are elementary tools, probably for estimates on determinants and Fredholm-type theory: Fredholm determinants, traces of exterior powers of nuclear operators, and Fredholm series in Banach spaces. That is consistent with Grothendieck's 1956 paper on Fredholm theory.
errors: The image shows the Gram entry $(a_i,a_j)=\sum_k a_{ik}\overline{a_{jk}}$ called the $(i,j)$ entry of something like ${}^tAA^*$. With this convention it is the $(i,j)$ entry of $AA^*$ (as the next page correctly writes); the determinant is unaffected.

Minor gap: in infinite dimension, $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix only if the basis is chosen to contain an orthonormal basis of $\mathrm{span}(a_1,\dots,a_n)$, adapted to the flag $\mathrm{span}(a_1)\subset\mathrm{span}(a_1,a_2)\subset\dots$. The dependent case (determinant $0$) should also be noted. The text gestures at this choice ('on peut choisir la base de façon que A soit triangulaire'), so this is a gap in exposition only.
Exponent in (5): the norm equals $\det(\mathrm{Gram})^{1/2}$. The handwriting is ambiguous, but the correct reading is $1/2$.

ideas.where_published: Possibly used implicitly in Grothendieck's 'La théorie de Fredholm' (Bull. SMF 1956) and the Mémoir AMS 16 (1955); exact presentation unsure

ideas.where_published: Hadamard-type bounds are used in Grothendieck's Fredholm theory paper (1956) to estimate Fredholm determinant coefficients

deep.surprise_reason: Entirely standard textbook material: exterior powers of a Hilbert space, Gram determinant, and Hadamard's inequality with the classical triangular-basis proof. It is presumably preparatory to Fredholm-determinant estimates. Nothing new or uncredited.
